title: burst-aware-kv-costbreakdown-probe-march-2026
abstract: Exploratory workbook analyzing KV/prefix cache behavior under bursty vs steady workloads. Quantifies token-level cost impact of different hit-rate improvements during microbursts and steady-state, and surfaces latency/eviction tradeoffs. Intended as a decision input for a conservative rollout of burst-aware prefetching + adaptive TTLs.
assumptions: Host inference token cost baseline = $0.0000125 per token (aligned to hosted API internal unit)
Baseline model throughput profile: 60M tokens/day across fleet, average request length 75 tokens, average seq_len 128 for per-request accounting
Burst events: 10% of daily traffic occurs in 5% of time windows (microbursts), peak qps during bursts is 6x steady qps
KV/prefix cache baseline hit-rate: steady 42%, burst 28% (cold windows due to unique prefixes)
Optimized config target hit-rate uplift: +12–28 percentage points depending on prefetch aggressiveness and TTL expansion
Latency penalty when expanding TTL or prefetching aggressively: +5–45 ms P95 depending on bucket and GPU affinity
Eviction budget constraint: total kv memory expansion capped at +30% for Dedicated pools without hardware changes

key_findings: Small hit-rate improvements during microbursts produce disproportionate cost savings: in our sample burst window scenario a lift from 28% to 56% cuts burst token spend by ~60% even though bursts are a small fraction of time.

Overall percent savings scale with burst concentration: customers with more bursty traffic (higher peak/median ratio) capture more benefit from burst-aware prefetching than uniformly steady workloads.
Memory headroom constraint is the most binding operational limit; >20% effective memory growth requires either eviction policy changes or Dedicated capacity bumps.
There is diminishing returns above ~65% hit-rate for common request distributions — extra prefetch effort yields smaller marginal savings while adding latency risk.
Conservative prefetching (moderate TTL expansion + targeted prefix grouping) yields predictable savings with minimal P95 latency impact and fits within current memory budgets for most customers.
recommendations: Pilot split: run burst-aware prefetching for 5% of production traffic targeted at 3 customers with high burstiness (identify via qps distribution metric) for 4 weeks.
Metrics to track: token cost per 1000 requests, hit-rate by prefix-age bucket, P50/P95 latency, memory utilization on Dedicated pools, error-rate changes post-prefetch.
Config knobs: per-customer TTL multiplier (1.0–1.3), prefetch depth (number of prefix variants), adaptive backoff when CPU/GPU scheduling pressure observed.
Rollout gating: only enable aggressive TTL expansion if memory growth <= 18% during pilot and P95 latency increase <= 12% relative.
Engineering ask: small runtime counter added to requests to tag "burst-prefetch" decisions and expose hit-rate by tag for observability (console dashboard tile + logging).
Product ask: add a billing simulation view in the Console showing projected monthly savings for a customer given observed burstiness and proposed hit-rate uplift options.
notes: Next steps: 1) Identify 3 pilot customers and create feature flags (JIRA-OPT-4123). 2) Build a small telemetry slice to emit hit-rate by prefix-age and burst-tag (Confluence-9876 has instrumentation spec). 3) Run a 4-week pilot and collect distributional metrics (expected pilot start: 2026-04-01). Open questions: long-tail prefixes that are user-specific (per-user caches) may need a separate eviction tier; caching across model variants requires cross-compatibility keys. See linked PR for initial simulation code.
